displayQuote: What does not kill me makes me stronger

meta.title: Who really said "What does not kill me makes me stronger"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — it’s really Nietzsche. Aphorism 8 of “Maxims and Arrows” in Twilight of the Idols (1888): “Was mich nicht umbringt, macht mich stärker.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'What does not kill me makes me stronger'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Nietzsche: aphorism 8 of Twilight of the Idols (1888). But it’s usually misquoted as ‘us’ or ‘you,’ not the original ‘me.’

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is genuinely Nietzsche. It is aphorism 8 of the “Maxims and Arrows” section of Twilight of the Idols (Götzen-Dämmerung, 1888): “Was mich nicht umbringt, macht mich stärker.” The popular English is a near-literal rendering of that line.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Anthony M. Ludovici, 1911 (“That which does not kill me, makes me stronger”)

source.excerpt: Aus der Kriegsschule des Lebens. — Was mich nicht umbringt, macht mich stärker. (“Out of life’s school of war — what does not kill me makes me stronger.”)
trail: Wikipedia ↗ traces the line to aphorism 8 of “Maxims and Arrows” in Twilight of the Idols (1888): “Was mich nicht umbringt, macht mich stärker.”

The exact wording appears in Anthony Ludovici’s 1911 English translation on Project Gutenberg ↗ as “That which does not kill me, makes me stronger,” under the heading “From the military school of life.”
The German original was published in 1888, placing the source text firmly in the public domain.
source.excerptNote: The line is the whole of aphorism 8; its first clause — “from life’s school of war” — is almost always dropped in popular use.

source.rightsNote: The source work, Nietzsche’s Twilight of the Idols, was first published in German in 1888 — long in the public domain. Early English translations such as Anthony Ludovici’s (1911) are also public domain; the popular wording is a near-literal rendering of the 1888 German, though some specific modern translations remain under their own copyright.

author.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
author.heading: About Friedrich Nietzsche
author.bio: Friedrich Nietzsche was a German philosopher whose work on morality, power and the individual reshaped modern thought. Twilight of the Idols (1888) was among his last books before his 1889 breakdown, written as a rapid-fire “philosophy with a hammer.” Its opening “Maxims and Arrows” are terse aphorisms — one of which became this famous line.

misattribution.heading: Genuine quote, mangled wording
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Nietzsche is correct — but the line is one of the most-misquoted sentences in English. Nietzsche wrote “me,” and framed it as the survivor’s hard-won lesson, not a blanket promise.

items.scope: “That which does not kill us makes us stronger”
items.why: The most common English form swaps Nietzsche’s first-person “me” for a universal “us.” The original ↗ is singular: “Was mich nicht umbringt” — “what does not kill me.”

items.scope: “What doesn’t kill you makes you stronger”
items.why: The second-person “you” version was cemented by Kelly Clarkson’s 2011 hit “Stronger (What Doesn’t Kill You).” It captures the sentiment but is not Nietzsche’s wording.

misattribution.truthLine: The real line is Nietzsche’s own, from Twilight of the Idols (1888): “Was mich nicht umbringt, macht mich stärker ↗” — “What does not kill me makes me stronger.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The aphorism sits under the sub-heading “Aus der Kriegsschule des Lebens” — from life’s school of war. For Nietzsche it was not a feel-good slogan but a claim about how strong individuals metabolise suffering into growth; the dropped first clause and the shift to “us/you” have softened it into the motivational mantra it is today.
